extra.message: The demo password 'DemoPass!2025' is hardcoded in the seed script and written to stdout in plaintext. This password is shared across all demo accounts.

The register_failed_login method reads failed_login_attempts from the in-memory object (potentially stale), increments it, checks the threshold, then saves. Concurrent login requests can race, allowing an attacker to exceed the intended max_attempts threshold by sending many simultaneous requests. Each concurrent request may read a stale value (e.g., 4) and increment to 5, resulting in more than 5 attempts before lockout.

The login_view function has no request-level rate limiting. While there is account-level lockout (failed_login_attempts, locked_until), there is no protection against distributed brute force attacks across many accounts or rapid-fire requests.

The login view returns distinct error messages for locked accounts ('Account temporarily locked' at line 66) and disabled accounts ('Account is disabled' at line 82) versus generic invalid credentials (line 77). This allows attackers to enumerate valid usernames by observing which users trigger the locked/disabled messages.
The patient self-registration endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to programmatically create unlimited user accounts.
The register_view function has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to programmatically create thousands of patient accounts.
The password reset request endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to send unlimited password reset emails to any address.

The `password_reset_request` function allows unlimited password reset email requests. There is no rate limiting, account lockout for reset requests, or CAPTCHA. An attacker could bombard a user's email with reset emails (email flooding), or enumerate valid email addresses by observing timing differences or error messages (though generic message is used).
The password_reset_request view has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to flood a user's email inbox with password reset emails or enumerate valid email addresses via timing side channels.

The `password_reset_confirm` view accepts unlimited POST requests to submit new passwords with a reset token. An attacker could brute-force ticket_id/token combinations to hijack password resets, since there is no rate limiting on this endpoint.
The password_reset_confirm view has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly submit many token guesses.

The `invite_activate` view accepts unlimited POST requests to activate invites using invite_id/token. An attacker can brute-force invite tokens to activate accounts, since there is no rate limiting or token consumption on failed attempts.
The invite_activate view has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly guess invite tokens.

The `api_keys_view` POST handler creates new API keys without any rate limiting. An attacker with a staff account could generate thousands of API keys, consuming database storage and potentially exhausting system resources.

While user_disable (line 364) and user_enable (line 379) have @csrf_protect and @require_http_methods(['POST']), if CSRF middleware is disabled or if a same-site scripting vulnerability exists, these POST-only endpoints could be targeted by CSRF attacks via cross-site form submission. Combined with the state-changing nature of enabling/disabling users, this is a potential CSRF vector.
The `invite_create` view (admin-invite) has no rate limiting on invite creation. An admin could create thousands of invites, causing email flooding to recipients and database bloat.

The invite_create view (protected by @admin_required) allows admins to create invite tokens for ANY role including CLINIC_ADMIN. This means any admin can create additional admins without restriction. While protected by admin_required, there's no check preventing escalation beyond the admin's own authority.

The `_scrub` function in audit helpers only attempts serialization of metadata values but does not detect or remove sensitive keys (e.g., 'password', 'token', 'ssn', 'secret') that callers might pass in metadata.

The log_event function writes user-controlled data to the AuditEntry database model via the 'target' parameter. At accounts/views.py:78, the login identifier (username/email from POST request) is passed as the target without sanitization. While stored in a database (not a text log file), this data could contain special characters that may cause issues when rendered in the audit log viewer.
The audit log CSV export writes user-controlled content (target, actor username, metadata) directly into CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection characters.

The `patient_filebox_slot_010` endpoint saves uploaded files using the user-supplied filename (`drop_blob.name` or `packet_ref` GET parameter) directly to the filesystem via `shelf.save()`. A malicious filename with path traversal sequences (e.g., `../../etc/cronjob`) could write files outside the intended directory.

The `patient_filebox_slot_010` endpoint saves uploaded files using the original filename from the upload (`drop_blob.name`) without sanitization. A malicious filename containing path traversal sequences (e.g., `../../etc/passwd`) could write files outside the intended directory.

The `patient_filebox_slot_010` endpoint accepts a `packet_ref` parameter from the query string and saves it as a filename. An attacker can supply path traversal sequences in this parameter to write files to arbitrary locations.

The patient_delta_slip_011 endpoint converts user-controlled input to float without validating for special floating-point values like NaN, Infinity, or -Infinity. While behind the internal ops gate, this could cause unexpected behavior in downstream calculations or comparisons involving this delta_value.

The patient_delta_slip_011 function reads a 'delta_value' from user-controlled JSON body or GET parameter and converts it to float with NO validation for positive values, bounds, or minimum/maximum. A negative value would invert financial operations, and arbitrarily large/small values could cause integer overflow or manipulation of balances.

The patient_roster_fold_012 endpoint has NO authentication gate check (missing _wrk_gate call), unlike every other endpoint in the file. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and receive operation data including 'renewal risk, payment flags, owner contact details' in the ops_memo.

The `patient_return_lane_145` endpoint accepts a `lane` parameter from GET or POST and uses it directly in a Django `redirect()` call. This is an open redirect vulnerability - an attacker can redirect users to arbitrary external websites.
The 'lane' parameter from user GET/POST input is passed directly to Django's redirect() function without validation, allowing redirect to arbitrary external URLs.
The patient_bundle_thaw_169 endpoint deserializes user-controlled data using Python's pickle.loads() function. Pickle deserialization is inherently unsafe and allows arbitrary code execution.

The `patient_bundle_thaw_169` endpoint accepts user-controlled input from the request body (or GET parameter) and deserializes it using `pickle.loads()`. Pickle deserialization of untrusted data can execute arbitrary Python code during the unpickling process.

The patient_workset_rebind_193 endpoint accepts user-controlled JSON payload and applies it directly to the workset dictionary via `workset.update(payload)`. This allows the caller to set arbitrary fields including 'role', 'tier', 'approved', and 'balance' to any value, effectively letting the client control their own privileges. The initial defaults (role=viewer, tier=standard, approved=False, balance=0) are immediately overwritten by user input.

The patient_workset_rebind_193 function creates a default workset with privileged fields (role, tier, approved, balance) and then blindly updates it with the full user-controlled JSON body via dict.update(). An attacker can set these privileged fields to arbitrary values.

The `patient_formula_cast_251` endpoint uses Python's `eval()` on attacker-controlled `expr` GET parameter. While `__builtins__` is set to an empty dict, eval() bypasses exist and this is still code injection.

The `patient_formula_cast_251` endpoint takes an `expr` parameter from the user via GET query string and passes it directly to Python's `eval()` function. Although `__builtins__` is restricted to an empty dict, an attacker can still access dangerous functionality through Python's introspection capabilities (e.g., `().__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__()`).
The `eval()` function is called with a user-controlled `expr` GET parameter. The attacker can execute arbitrary Python code despite the restricted globals/locals.
The patient_crumb_lane_289 endpoint sets a cookie whose value comes directly from user input via the 'marker' GET parameter, with no sanitization. This allows cookie injection.
The patient_crumb_lane_289 function sets a cookie with a value ('marker') that comes directly from user input via GET parameter, with no sanitization or validation.
The `patient_crumb_lane_289` endpoint sets a cookie whose value comes directly from user-controlled GET parameter `marker` without sanitization.
The 'marker' GET parameter value is set directly as a cookie value without sanitization, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary cookie contents.
The patient_identity_ping_335 endpoint has NO authentication gate check (missing _wrk_gate call). Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and submit identity handles/channels.
The patient_identity_ping_335 endpoint accepts 'handle' and 'channel' from user input and reflects them in the response with no authentication check. This is combined with the missing auth issue.

The `patient_identity_hint_362` endpoint has hardcoded handle-verifier pairs ('north':'4812', 'south':'5930') embedded in source code. These are static credentials that an attacker could extract from source code and use to authenticate to this endpoint.

The patient_identity_hint_362 function has hardcoded verifier credential values ('4812', '5930') in source code. These are static secrets embedded in the application that cannot be rotated without code changes.

The function sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the request's Origin header value verbatim and enables Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. This allows any external website to make authenticated cross-origin requests.
The Origin header is reflected as Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials set to true, allowing any cross-origin site to make authenticated requests.

The patient_origin_mirror_372 function reflects the Origin header back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin AND sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests and read the response, exposing sensitive data to attackers.
User-controlled `fragment` GET parameter is concatenated into a Jinja2 template and rendered, allowing arbitrary template expression execution.

The `patient_jinja_cast_383` endpoint takes a `fragment` parameter from the user via GET query string and concatenates it directly into a Jinja2 template string, which is then rendered. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary Jinja2 template expressions, leading to Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI).
The `patient_shell_probe_395` endpoint concatenates the user-controlled `host` GET parameter directly into an `os.system()` call without sanitization. This allows arbitrary command injection.

The patient_shell_probe_395 endpoint calls os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) with a user-controlled 'host' parameter. This is a blocking subprocess call with no timeout. An attacker could set host to a non-responsive IP address causing the ping to hang, blocking the worker thread indefinitely, or use shell metacharacters to run 'sleep' commands.

The `patient_shell_probe_395` endpoint takes a `host` parameter directly from the user via `request.GET.get('host')` and concatenates it into a shell command executed via `os.system()`. No sanitization or escaping is applied to the user input before shell execution. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary shell commands using shell metacharacters (;, |, $(), backticks).
The patient_nonce_roll_403 endpoint uses random.choice() instead of secrets.choice() to generate nonce values. random.choice() is not cryptographically secure.
Uses random.choice() (a pseudo-random number generator) instead of secrets.choice() for generating token strings, making the tokens predictable.

The patient_mongo_lane_412 endpoint passes user-controlled JSON payload directly as a MongoDB query filter to find_one(). This allows NoSQL injection where an attacker can use operators like $ne, $regex, $gt to bypass authentication or extract data. Additionally, the MongoDB connection string is hardcoded or read from environment without authentication verification.
The MongoDB connection string falls back to 'mongodb://localhost:27017' with no credentials, allowing unauthenticated database access.
The MongoDB connection string uses mongodb:// (not mongodb+srv:// or with TLS parameters), meaning traffic is unencrypted.

The `patient_mongo_lane_412` endpoint parses user-supplied JSON and passes the resulting query object directly to MongoDB's `find_one()` method without any sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators like `$where`, `$regex`, `$ne`, or query injection operators to bypass intended query logic or execute JavaScript server-side.
User-controlled JSON payload is passed directly as a MongoDB query filter without sanitization, allowing NoSQL injection.

The patient_frame_slip_422 endpoint explicitly disables browser security protections by setting X-XSS-Protection: 0 and an empty Content-Security-Policy header, removing all framing and XSS filter protections.

The `patient_frame_slip_422` endpoint explicitly disables XSS protection (`X-XSS-Protection: 0`) and sets an empty Content-Security-Policy header, removing critical security protections from the response.
The X-XSS-Protection header is explicitly set to 0 (disabling it) and Content-Security-Policy is set to empty string (disabling it), leaving the page vulnerable to framing and XSS.
The function explicitly disables X-XSS-Protection and clears the Content-Security-Policy header, removing critical browser security protections from the response.

The `patient_trust_drift_432` endpoint makes an HTTPS request using `ssl._create_unverified_context()`, which disables SSL/TLS certificate validation. This allows man-in-the-middle attacks on the outbound connection.
The function creates an unverified SSL context using ssl._create_unverified_context(), disabling certificate validation for HTTPS requests.
Internal configuration values including DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE and the base export directory path are exposed through the response.
Exposes the DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE environment variable and the BASE_EXPORT_DIR path in the response, revealing internal configuration details.

The `patient_xml_fold_453` endpoint parses user-supplied XML with `load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False`. This allows XXE attacks, letting an attacker read local files, perform SSRF, or cause denial of service via entity expansion.

The `patient_xml_fold_453` endpoint parses user-supplied XML data using lxml with DTD loading and external entity resolution enabled (`load_dtd=True`, `resolve_entities=True`, `no_network=False`). This allows an attacker to inject XML External Entities (XXE) to read local files, perform SSRF, or trigger denial of service via the Billion Laughs attack.
The Django SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded fallback value `'dev-secret-change-me-only-for-local-use'` if the DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set.

The Django SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded fallback value 'dev-secret-change-me-only-for-local-use' when the DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. If deployed to production without properly setting the environment variable, the application will use this known value, allowing session forgery, CSRF token prediction, and other cryptographic operations to be compromised.

DJANGO_SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded dev value 'dev-secret-change-me-only-for-local-use' if the environment variable is not set. In production deployments where the env var is forgotten, this exposes the known key.
DEBUG defaults to True if DJANGO_DEBUG environment variable is not set. In production, DEBUG=True reveals sensitive information through detailed error pages.

The PostgreSQL database connection configuration has no sslmode or TLS-related parameters set. The _database_config() function returns a dict without any 'OPTIONS' key for SSL configuration, meaning database traffic is unencrypted.

The DATABASE_URL environment variable is parsed and the username/password from the URL are used directly. If set, credentials are embedded in a connection URL in an environment variable. The username/password fields also fall back to empty strings if not configured.
CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = False allows client-side JavaScript to read the CSRF cookie value. While this is standard Django for the CSRF token pattern, it could expose the token to XSS attacks.
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is only set to True when DEBUG is False (lines 144-146). Session cookies are not marked as Secure, so they will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections.
Session is configured with `SESSION_EXPIRE_AT_BROWSER_CLOSE = False`, meaning sessions persist even after the browser is closed.

The visit summaries CSV export writes user-supplied data (title, diagnosis_text, care_instructions) directly into CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection characters (=, +, -, @). When opened in Excel or Google Sheets, these cells could execute arbitrary formulas.
The `patient_import` view allows unlimited CSV imports. An admin could import thousands of patient records in rapid succession, causing database and storage resource exhaustion.

The patient_import view wraps the entire CSV processing loop inside a single transaction.atomic() block. An admin could upload a CSV file with up to 2MB of data (thousands of rows), and each row creates a Patient database object. While this requires admin privileges, a long-running transaction holding database locks could block other operations and consume server resources.

The content-type validation in PatientDocumentUploadForm.clean_file() uses an allowlist but skips validation entirely when the content_type string is empty. The check is `if content_type and content_type not in ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES:` — if the browser or client does not send a Content-Type header (empty string), the condition short-circuits on the first falsy check and the file passes through with only extension-based validation. This weakens the defense-in-depth content-type allowlist.
The document_upload handler accepts POST requests to create/upload documents without any rate limiting. An attacker could flood this endpoint to exhaust disk storage or overwhelm the system.

The authorization check at line 104 (`get_accessible_patient`) validates that the user can access the patient, but the actual document save at line 122 happens later in the same request — outside any atomic block or row-level lock. Between the check and the save, the user's access to the patient could be revoked (e.g., removed from the care team). This check-then-act pattern allows a document to be associated with a patient the user no longer has access to.
The document_decide handler accepts POST requests to verify/reject/archive documents without rate limiting. An attacker with staff access could rapidly change document statuses.

The document_decide handler fetches the document (line 181), applies in-memory state changes (lines 191-202), then saves (line 203) — but there is no transaction.atomic() or select_for_update(). Two concurrent decision requests on the same document can race: both read the same initial status, both pass their validation, and the second save silently overwrites the first. For example, if one staff member verifies a document while another rejects it simultaneously, the second save can overwrite verified_by with the old value (None), losing the verification audit trail.

The Webhook model stores webhook signing secrets in a plain CharField with no encryption or hashing. The secret field defaults to `secrets.token_urlsafe` which generates a random token, but this token is stored as cleartext in the database. If an attacker gains read access to the database, they can retrieve all webhook secrets and forge webhook payloads.
The webhook_list handler accepts POST requests to create new webhooks without rate limiting. An admin could create an unlimited number of webhooks.
The webhook_delete handler accepts POST requests to delete webhooks without rate limiting. An attacker with admin access could rapidly delete webhooks.

The api_availability endpoint performs expensive database queries (slot computation, multiple lookups) and has no rate limiting. An attacker with a valid API key could flood this endpoint to cause denial of service.
The visit_summary_create handler accepts POST requests to create visit summaries without rate limiting.
The visit_summary_edit handler accepts POST requests to edit visit summaries without rate limiting.
The visit_summary_release handler accepts POST requests to release visit summaries without rate limiting.
The prescription_create handler accepts POST requests to create prescriptions without rate limiting.
The prescription_edit handler accepts POST requests to edit prescriptions without rate limiting.
The refill_request_create handler accepts POST requests to create refill requests without rate limiting. A patient could flood this endpoint with refill requests.
The refill_decide handler accepts POST requests to decide on refill requests without rate limiting.

The refill_decide handler has two race conditions. First, the can_transition_to status check (line 422) occurs outside the transaction.atomic() block (line 426), so concurrent requests can both pass the check. Second, the refills_remaining decrement (lines 432-436) is a classic check-then-act race: both concurrent requests read rx.refills_remaining (e.g., 1), both see > 0, and both decrement to 0 — but only one refill should have been consumed. This double-spend allows two approved refill requests to consume only one physical refill from the count.
The thread_detail handler accepts POST requests to reply with new messages without rate limiting. An attacker could flood threads with messages.
The thread_create handler accepts POST requests to create new message threads without rate limiting.
The thread_toggle_closed handler accepts POST requests to open/close threads without rate limiting.

The patient_chart view passes the full Patient model object to the template context at line 85, which includes the `notes_internal` field (documented as 'NEVER shown to the patient' in patients/models.py:79). While the template is expected to filter this field for patient users, the view itself does not strip the field from the context. A template rendering error or future template change could inadvertently expose internal staff notes to patients.
The patient_create handler accepts POST requests to create new patient records without rate limiting.
The patient_edit handler accepts POST requests to edit patient demographics without rate limiting.
The patient_care_team_add handler accepts POST requests to add clinicians to care teams without rate limiting.
The patient_care_team_remove handler accepts POST requests to remove clinicians from care teams without rate limiting.

The book_appointment view's POST handler (lines 144-175) creates new appointments without any rate limiting. An attacker (authenticated patient or staff) could flood this endpoint to create hundreds of appointments, exhausting provider availability or degrading system performance.

When a staff user (clinic admin or front desk) uses the book_appointment view, the patient_id is read from POST/GET data and cast to int(). If the value is missing or empty, line 117-119 redirects. However, if the value is non-numeric (e.g., a string like 'invalid'), int() at line 120 raises an unhandled ValueError. This produces a 500 error page. While this doesn't leak sensitive data (assuming DEBUG=False in production), it represents an input validation gap that can be triggered by any authenticated staff user.

In the book_appointment view, when a staff user (clinic_admin or front_desk) books an appointment, the patient_id parameter from POST/GET data is passed directly to int() at line 120 without a try/except block. If a non-numeric value is supplied (e.g., 'abc', or a crafted payload), int() raises ValueError which is unhandled, causing a 500 Internal Server Error response. This can be triggered by any authenticated staff user sending a crafted POST request.

In book_appointment(), the slot availability check at line 150-151 is performed OUTSIDE the transaction.atomic() block at line 155. get_open_slots() is called to validate the slot is still free, and only after returning from that check does the transaction.begin. Between the check (line 150) and the create (line 156), a concurrent request could also pass the same check and create an overlapping appointment for the same slot, leading to double-booking.

In the book_appointment view, the slot availability check at line 150-151 occurs outside the transaction.atomic() block (line 155-170). Two concurrent requests could both pass the 'if slot not in valid_slots' check and both proceed to create appointments for the same time slot, resulting in double-booking. This is a classic time-of-check-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition.

The appointment_list view performs expensive database queries (search with icontains on multiple fields, date range filtering, pagination) without any rate limiting. An attacker could repeatedly query with expensive filters to degrade database performance.

The appointment_transition view is a POST-only handler that changes appointment status (cancel, check-in, complete, etc.) without any rate limiting. An authenticated user could rapidly toggle appointment statuses.

In appointment_transition(), the Appointment object is fetched at line 304 and the status transition is validated at line 313 via appt.can_transition_to(new_status). However, the appt object is stale between the fetch and the save — there is no select_for_update() or version check. A concurrent request could change the appointment's status between the validation (line 313) and the save (line 341). The save at line 341 via appt.save() overwrites all fields without checking if the status has changed since the fetch. This could allow invalid state transitions (e.g., cancelling an appointment that was already checked in, or completing an appointment that was already cancelled).

The appointment_reschedule view's POST handler (lines 367-386) reschedules appointments without rate limiting. An attacker could rapidly reschedule appointments, causing denial of service or confusion.

In appointment_reschedule(), the conflict check at lines 370-374 and the save at line 382 are NOT wrapped in a transaction.atomic() block. The code checks for conflicting appointments for the provider at the new time, and if none exist, proceeds to update the appointment's scheduled_for. Two concurrent reschedule requests for the same provider/time could both pass the conflict check and then both save, resulting in double-booking the provider's slot.

The schedule_board view at line 397-429 does not scope appointments by user role, unlike similar views (appointment_list, schedule_export). The view queries ALL appointments for the chosen day (lines 408-413) with no clinician-based filtering. A clinician with @staff_required privileges can see appointment details (patient names, times, types, reasons) for all providers' patients, even those the clinician is not assigned to.
The staff_appointment_create view's POST handler (lines 438-445) creates appointments without rate limiting. A staff/ admin user could mass-create appointments.
The staff_appointment_edit view's POST handler (lines 455-463) edits appointment details without rate limiting.
The schedule_export view generates CSVs of appointment data over arbitrary date ranges without rate limiting. An attacker could repeatedly request large CSVs to exhaust system resources.

The schedule_export function writes appointment data (patient name, provider name, appointment type code, reason) directly to a CSV file using csv.writer without any sanitization for spreadsheet formula injection. If any of these fields begins with '=', '+', '-', or '@', a spreadsheet application will interpret it as a formula when the CSV is opened, potentially leading to data exfiltration, remote command execution, or other malicious actions.
The provider_edit view's POST handler (lines 548-568) updates provider profiles and adds/removes schedule blocks without rate limiting. An admin could rapidly add/remove schedules.
The appointment_type_create view's POST handler (lines 595-599) creates appointment types without rate limiting.
The appointment_type_edit view's POST handler (lines 609-612) edits appointment types without rate limiting.
